strengths: Introduces a novel and practically motivated task of combining pixel-level forgery localization with natural-language interpretation, moving beyond binary masks.

Constructs a large-scale (128,303 triplet) multimodal dataset (MMTT) spanning face-swap and two inpainting-based manipulation types, with paired binary masks and human-written textual explanations, filling a genuine gap versus existing forgery datasets that lack text annotations.
The annotation pipeline (minimum inspection time, maximum caption length, false-positive screening, two-phase relabeling) is reasonably well documented and shows some care for quality control.

The proposed ForgeryTalker architecture (Forgery Prompter Network + Mask Decoder + MLLM) is a sensible combination of existing building blocks (CoordConv, SAM decoder, InstructBLIP) tailored to the new task, and the ablations (w/ FPN-GT, w/o FPN, loss/ω study) provide some insight into which components matter.
Comprehensive comparison table situates MMTT among prior forgery/deepfake datasets, clarifying its relative novelty (mask + text annotation).
weaknesses: The core empirical gains are marginal and inconsistent: ForgeryTalker's CIDEr (21.5) barely exceeds InstructBLIP (20.9), and its IoU (70.81) is actually lower than SCA's (72.87); across most metrics differences are within a point or two, so the claimed 'superior performance' is not well substantiated.

The central mechanism (Forgery Prompter Network) that is supposed to drive interpretability achieves only 41% PLM accuracy, meaning the region prompts guiding explanation generation are frequently wrong; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not adequately address how this affects the reliability/faithfulness of the generated interpretations.

No human evaluation or faithfulness/hallucination analysis of the generated textual interpretations is provided; automated captioning metrics (CIDEr/BLEU/METEOR) do not verify whether explanations are actually correct or grounded in the true manipulation, which is the paper's key claimed contribution.

Experimental setup for baselines (SCA, LISA-7B, Osprey, InstructBLIP) is underspecified — it is unclear whether these were fine-tuned on MMTT or used zero/few-shot, which is critical for a fair comparison and for reproducibility.

No inter-annotator agreement statistics, annotator training/qualification details, or analysis of annotation consistency are reported despite 30 annotators contributing free-text descriptions over an extended period; 'simple screening' for quality control is minimally described.

The dataset construction relies entirely on synthetic manipulations from a small set of automatic methods (E4S, MAT, SDXL) on two source datasets (CelebA-HQ, FFHQ); generalization to real-world/in-the-wild deepfakes or unseen manipulation methods is untested.

No discussion of dual-use/ethical risks despite building a deepfake dataset and pipeline explicitly annotated with realistic manipulation cues, which could itself be misused to improve forgery evasion.

Fit to the ACL/NLP venue is questionable: the paper is fundamentally a computer-vision forgery-localization contribution with a captioning component; the linguistic/NLP contribution (caption generation via an off-the-shelf MLLM) is comparatively thin and not analyzed from a language-quality or discourse perspective.
Statistical robustness is limited — single-run results with no variance/significance testing, and the mask decoder and Q-former results in Table 2 lack error bars.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored problem: coupling pixel-level forgery localization with free-text interpretive explanations, which could be a useful step beyond binary tamper masks.

The MMTT dataset is large in raw numbers (128,303 image-text-mask triplets) and combines several manipulation pipelines (GAN-based face swapping, transformer- and diffusion-based inpainting), giving some diversity of forgery types.

The proposed ForgeryTalker architecture (Forgery Prompter Network + Mask Decoder + MLLM) is a reasonable engineering combination of existing building blocks (SAM decoder, InstructBLIP, CoordConv) tailored to the joint localization/explanation task.
The paper includes some ablations (FPN vs. no FPN vs. GT labels; loss/ω choices) that attempt to isolate the contribution of individual components.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim of "superior performance" is not well supported: ForgeryTalker's gains over InstructBLIP are marginal (e.g., CIDEr 21.5 vs 20.9, BLEU-4 5.9 vs 5.6), and it is clearly outperformed by SCA on IoU (70.81 vs 72.87) and by InstructBLIP on recall and ROUGE-L. No significance testing or variance/error bars are reported, so these small deltas cannot be judged as meaningful.

The ablation in Table 3 reveals that using oracle FPN labels nearly doubles CIDEr (48.1 vs 21.5), while the actual learned FPN only reaches 41% PLM (Table 4) — this shows the core technical module that is supposed to drive interpretability is far from reliable, undermining the paper's claimed contribution and suggesting the reported gains largely reflect a weak, noisy prompter rather than a validated mechanism.

Annotation quality control is thin and underspecified: only "minimum time" and "simple screening for false positives" are described; there is no inter-annotator agreement study, no reported annotator qualifications/training beyond "expert team," and no analysis of annotation consistency or bias, which is critical for a dataset whose main novelty is human-authored textual interpretations.

No human evaluation of the generated interpretive captions' correctness, faithfulness, or usefulness is provided; only automatic n-gram metrics (CIDEr/BLEU/ROUGE) are used, which are known to be weak proxies for whether an explanation actually identifies the correct, salient manipulated characteristics — a serious gap for a paper whose main motivation is interpretability.

The dataset and method are restricted entirely to frontal/aligned facial images from two curated sources (CelebA-HQ, FFHQ) with only three synthetic manipulation methods (E4S, MAT, SDXL); the claim of being a general "large-scale" benchmark for facial forgery localization somewhat overstates the diversity (no real-world/in-the-wild deepfakes, no video, limited manipulation variety) relative to prior datasets like ForgeryNet or DF40 cited in the same table.

The Related Work section is thin, loosely organized (e.g., segmentation and classification methods lumped under an "Interpretation Annotation" heading despite not addressing interpretation), and does not engage with other interpretable/explainable deepfake detection or VQA-style forensic works beyond citation lists.

Reproducibility cannot currently be verified: dataset, code, and checkpoints are only promised for future release, not provided with the submission, and several implementation choices (e.g., discount factor, FPN architecture specifics) are given without ablation sensitivity beyond a small table.

The comparison baselines (SCA, LISA, Osprey, InstructBLIP) are general-purpose segmentation/captioning or reasoning-segmentation models not designed for forgery detection, raising questions about whether the comparison fairly isolates the contribution of the proposed forgery-specific modules versus simply fine-tuning on the new dataset.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task—interpretable forgery localization that pairs pixel-level masks with textual explanations—filling a clear gap in prior binary-mask-only forgery localization work.

Contributes a large-scale (128,303 triplets) multi-modal dataset (MMTT) spanning three manipulation types (GAN-based face swapping, transformer- and diffusion-based inpainting), with a described human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline including time constraints, length constraints, and a quality-control/screening step.
Provides a thorough comparison against ten existing forgery datasets (Table 1), clearly positioning MMTT's novelty (combined mask + text annotation) relative to prior work.

Proposes a reasonably detailed architecture (Forgery Prompter Network + Mask Decoder + MLLM) with ablations isolating the contribution of the FPN and the effect of loss/hyperparameter choices (Table 4).
Releases (promised) code, dataset, and checkpoints, supporting reproducibility if delivered as stated.
weaknesses: The dataset is built entirely from synthetically manipulated images (E4S face swapping, MAT/SDXL inpainting) rather than in-the-wild or diverse deepfake generators; no cross-dataset generalization experiment (e.g., FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF) is reported to validate that textual/mask annotations transfer beyond this constructed distribution.

No inter-annotator agreement, annotator qualification, or subjectivity/bias analysis is reported for the 30 annotators, despite textual interpretation being inherently subjective (which artifacts count as 'salient' can vary across annotators)—this is a key reproducibility/soundness gap for a dataset whose central contribution is human-authored explanation.

The core empirical claims are only marginally supported: ForgeryTalker's gains over InstructBLIP are small (e.g., CIDEr 21.5 vs 20.9, BLEU-1 31.1 vs 30.6) and no significance testing or multiple-run variance is reported, making it hard to conclude the proposed FPN/Mask Decoder components meaningfully improve over a strong existing baseline.

The FPN itself performs poorly (PLM only 41%), and the paper's own ablation shows that with ground-truth region prompts the CIDEr jumps to 48.1 versus 21.5 with predicted prompts—indicating that the current pipeline is far from realizing its stated benefit, and the paper explicitly defers this to 'future work' rather than resolving it.

Evaluation of the explanation-generation task relies solely on n-gram overlap metrics (CIDEr, BLEU, METEOR/ROUGE), which are known to correlate weakly with factual correctness; there is no human evaluation or faithfulness/factual-consistency assessment of whether the generated interpretations actually correspond to real manipulation artifacts, which is critical given interpretability/trustworthiness is the paper's central motivation.

Some baselines (SCA, Osprey) are not forgery-specific, and IoU comparisons are somewhat apples-to-oranges (e.g., SCA relies on SAM, acknowledged in the text as giving it an unfair localization advantage), weakening the strength of the comparative claims.

Related Work Section 2.1 is mislabeled 'Interpretation Annotation' but its subsections discuss unrelated topics (facial manipulation localization, multi-label classification, segmentation techniques) without substantively engaging prior interpretable/explainable forgery detection literature, suggesting incomplete positioning within the interpretability literature.

No discussion of ethical/dual-use considerations around releasing techniques and models capable of localized facial manipulation alongside interpretive captions, which is relevant given the sensitive nature of deepfake research.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task (joint forgery localization + natural language explanation) that goes beyond binary/pixel-level forgery detection toward interpretable forensics.

Constructs a large-scale dataset (152,217 samples) spanning three manipulation paradigms (face swapping, face editing, inpainting) with process-derived pixel-perfect masks and human-authored textual descriptions, filling a genuine gap versus existing forgery datasets that lack rich text annotation (Table 1 comparison is informative).
Provides a reasonably detailed annotation pipeline with explicit guidelines, minimum observation time, maximum length constraints, and automated false-positive-region flagging for quality control.

Proposes a coherent baseline architecture (ForgeryTalker) with a clearly described two-stage training procedure (forgery-aware pretraining + attribution generation) and ablates its components (FPN, pretraining stage) showing consistent, interpretable gains.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple settings: zero-shot large VLMs, fine-tuned specialist baselines, cross-dataset generalization (DQ_F++, SynthScars), and a fine-grained ablation on manipulation-type contribution, which strengthens the empirical case for the proposed baseline's competitiveness.

Reasonable reproducibility documentation (implementation details, training protocol, planned release of code/data/checkpoints) and explicit ethical statement addressing dual-use risks of releasing forged-face data.
weaknesses: The core novelty of the task -- generating trustworthy 'why' explanations -- is evaluated only with n-gram/overlap metrics (CIDEr, BLEU, ROUGE-L); there is no human evaluation of explanation correctness, faithfulness, or hallucination rate, which is a significant soundness gap given the stated goal of building reviewer trust in the forensic report.

No inter-annotator agreement or independent quality audit is reported for the human-authored descriptions despite 30 annotators producing over 150K annotations; the example descriptions in Figure 7 appear formulaic/templated, raising questions about the actual linguistic diversity and independence of annotations from the mask-guided instructions.

The explanations are described as 'grounded in the editing process,' but annotators only describe visually observed artifacts within the (given) ground-truth mask region -- this is appearance-based description, not causal grounding in the actual generative editing pipeline, so the framing somewhat overstates what the text captures.

The large gap between the oracle-prompted variant (FPN-GT: 95.1 CIDEr) and the actual learned-FPN system (59.3 CIDEr) shows that most of the system's report quality is bottlenecked by inaccurate region prediction; this limitation is only mentioned briefly and undercuts claims of a strong end-to-end baseline.

Manipulation methods used to build the dataset (E4S, StyleCLIP, HFGI, MAT, SDXL) are relatively dated/limited compared to current SOTA generative editing tools, and there is no evaluation of cross-domain generalization to real-world or unconstrained deepfakes (e.g., FaceForensics++-style manipulations in the wild), limiting the demonstrated ecological validity of the benchmark.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is not fully established -- it is unclear whether all fine-tuned baselines (SCA, LISA, Osprey, FFAA, FakeShield) were tuned with comparable effort/hyperparameter search, and no variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for any experiment.

The paper's contribution is primarily a computer-vision forensics dataset and multimodal captioning baseline; the NLP-specific contribution (beyond producing template-like descriptive captions) is relatively thin, raising questions about centrality to a computational linguistics venue.

Some reported numbers across tables show apparent inconsistencies (e.g., certain BLEU-4/ROUGE-L orderings for FFAA/FakeShield in Table 2 look anomalous), suggesting the results tables may contain errors that were not caught during preparation.

strengths: The MMTT dataset is large-scale (152,217 samples) and is the first resource to pair process-derived, pixel-precise forgery masks with human-written natural-language explanations spanning three manipulation paradigms (face swap, face editing, inpainting), filling a genuine gap relative to existing binary-label or mask-only forgery datasets (Table 1).

The paper defines a reasonably well-motivated new task (joint 'where' and 'why' forgery attribution) and provides a complete pipeline: dataset construction, annotation protocol with quality control, a baseline architecture (ForgeryTalker) with a two-stage training regime, and a fairly extensive battery of experiments (zero-shot LVLM comparison, fine-tuned specialist baselines, cross-dataset generalization on DQ_F++ and SynthScars, several ablations).

The ablation studies (FPN, pretraining stage, manipulation-type leave-one-out, PLM metric analysis) go beyond a single headline result and attempt to isolate the contribution of individual design choices, which is good practice for a baseline/resource paper.

Reasonably clear documentation of ethical considerations (controlled dataset release, DUA, screening of source images) and a reproducibility statement with implementation details (hyperparameters, compute, split ratios).
weaknesses: Annotation methodology is circular with respect to the stated goal: annotators are shown the ground-truth mask and explicitly instructed to describe artifacts only within the already-known manipulated region. This means the textual 'why' explanations are not independently discovered evidence of manipulation but after-the-fact descriptions conditioned on a privileged oracle signal, which the deployed model never has access to. This undermines the claim that the dataset/text captures genuine diagnostic reasoning about 'why' an image is a forgery versus simply describing masked-region appearance, and raises concerns about how well performance will transfer to real-world settings where no mask is available a priori.

The qualitative examples (Figure 6, Figure 7) show highly templated, repetitive phrasing ('asymmetrical eyebrows,' 'blurry,' 'lacking real skin texture,' 'contours are not clear') across very different images, suggesting the textual annotations may have limited diversity/informativeness despite the claimed '4 million words' corpus; this is not adequately quantified (e.g., no measure of description diversity, factual grounding, or inter-annotator agreement on textual content, only on timing/region constraints).

Evaluation of the explanation-generation subtask relies solely on n-gram overlap metrics (CIDEr, BLEU, ROUGE-L), which do not assess factual correctness or faithfulness of the generated 'why' explanation to the actual artifact present. For a task centrally motivated by trustworthiness and interpretability, the absence of any human evaluation or faithfulness/groundedness metric is a significant evidentiary gap.

Table 2 contains internally inconsistent/anomalous numbers for FFAA and FakeShield (BLEU-4 values of 12.9 and 12.3 are higher than their respective BLEU-3 values of 4.0 and 2.3, violating the expected monotonic decrease of n-gram precision with n and strongly suggesting a column-alignment or transcription error). This calls into question the care taken in reporting baseline results and the overall reliability of the comparison table.

Table 9's 'w/o Image Inpainting' row shows ROUGE-L collapsing to 2.70 while BLEU-1 remains at 25.00, an implausible combination for coherent generated text, again suggesting an unflagged data/reporting error rather than a genuine finding, and this anomaly is not discussed or sanity-checked in the text.

The architectural contribution (InstructBLIP backbone + SAM-style mask decoder + a ViT/Conv hybrid prompter network) is largely a recombination of existing well-known components (Q-Former, SAM Two-way Transformer, CoordConv, contrastive and MLM losses); the novelty is primarily in task framing and data rather than methodology, which is acceptable for a baseline paper but is oversold in places as a 'unified framework...enabling coherent cross-modal reasoning.'

The manipulation methods used to build MMTT (E4S, StyleCLIP, HFGI, MAT, SDXL) are not uniformly state-of-the-art/diverse compared to current high-fidelity diffusion-based face forgery pipelines, and the very high localization scores (IoU up to 73-92% precision) suggest the forged/pristine boundary may be comparatively easy relative to more adversarial real-world deepfakes, which could limit the benchmark's long-term utility and inflate reported baseline-beating numbers.

Fit for an NLP/ACL venue is questionable: the textual contribution is a short, templated region-description generation task evaluated with captioning metrics, with limited linguistic complexity or novel NLP methodology; the paper reads primarily as a computer-vision forensics contribution with a modest multimodal captioning component.

No clear explanation is given for why some strong baselines (FFAA, FakeShield) perform so poorly (CIDEr around 10-17 versus 59.3 for the proposed model) — whether this reflects genuine capability gaps or inadequate adaptation/prompting of baselines to the new task format, which affects the fairness and interpretability of the comparison.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated new task (joint forgery localization + natural-language attribution) that meaningfully extends prior binary/mask-only forensics work toward interpretability.

Presents a genuinely large-scale resource (152,217 samples) spanning three manipulation paradigms with process-derived pixel-perfect masks and human-authored descriptions, which is a real contribution to the community given the scarcity of paired mask+text forgery data.

The proposed ForgeryTalker architecture (shared encoder, Forgery Prompter Network, dual mask/text decoders, two-stage training) is reasonably well described and technically coherent, integrating segmentation and captioning within a single InstructBLIP-based framework.

Experiments are fairly extensive: comparisons against zero-shot LVLMs and multiple fine-tuned specialist baselines, plus generalization tests on two external datasets (DQ_F++, SynthScars) and several ablations (FPN necessity, pretraining stage, per-manipulation-type contribution, loss/discount-factor choices for FPN).

Reasonably thorough documentation of dataset construction (mask generation formulas for each manipulation type), quality-control procedures for annotation, and a clear reproducibility/ethics statement with dataset-access safeguards.
weaknesses: The annotation protocol has a potential circularity concern: annotators are shown the ground-truth mask before writing the textual explanation, which may cause descriptions to be conditioned on/leak the localization answer rather than reflecting independent forensic reasoning; this undermines the claimed complementarity of the 'where' and 'why' subtasks and the interpretive value of the generated text.

No human evaluation of explanation quality, faithfulness, or factual correctness is reported. Automatic n-gram metrics (CIDEr/BLEU/ROUGE) are known to be weak indicators of whether generated forensic explanations are actually accurate or trustworthy, which is central to the paper's motivating claim about increasing user 'trust.'

There are unexplained numerical inconsistencies between the main results table (Table 2: IoU 73.67, CIDEr 59.3 for the full ForgeryTalker) and the manipulation-type ablation table (Table 9: Full Set IoU 71.00, CIDEr 56.90), which raises reproducibility and experimental-protocol clarity concerns.

Generalization results on SynthScars are very weak in absolute terms (CIDEr ~2.2), and while attributed to stylistic domain shift, this substantially undercuts the claim of strong cross-dataset generalization and is not further diagnosed (e.g., via human/qualitative analysis of failure modes).

No discussion of demographic bias despite using CelebAMask-HQ/FFHQ (known to have skewed demographic distributions), which is particularly relevant for a facial forensics dataset intended for broad forensic use.

Task framing explicitly avoids real/fake binary classification, citing that existing detectors already saturate that task; however, this leaves ForgeryTalker's practical deployment story incomplete, since a full forensic pipeline would still need a preceding detection step not evaluated here.

Limited analysis of failure cases or error diversity beyond a few qualitative examples; no variance/error bars across runs to support the significance of the reported metric gains over strong baselines like InstructBLIP.
